structure.rationale: The ten user-supplied chapters (kept in the requester's order) move from the frame to the machinery to the system: first the architectural principles every later trade-off is judged against (layering, end-to-end, fate sharing, control/data/management planes, per Saltzer-Reed-Clark and Clark '88); then the data plane inside one box (forwarding), then how many boxes agree on paths (routing), then how endpoints share those paths (transport) and how the network arbitrates contention (queues, AQM, scheduling, QoS). Security follows once the reader knows every mechanism an attacker can abuse. SDN, virtualization/cloud and wireless/edge are three re-arrangements of the same planes under new constraints (central control, multi-tenancy, scarce and moving capacity). Measurement and operations close the loop and host the capstone case studies, which reuse every earlier chapter.
structure.audience: Expert readers who already understand fundamental networking (packets, IP addressing, the layer model, basic TCP); they want architectural trade-offs, protocol internals, quantitative reasoning, security, virtualization and operational practice — delivered in the thing-explainer plain-words voice without losing technical precision.

claims.text: Layering gives each layer a service interface to the one above and hides how the layer below works, so implementations can change independently; the Internet's stack is often drawn as an hourglass with IP as the narrow waist.

Akhshabi & Dovrolis's EvoArch model reproduces the hourglass shape from almost any starting stack; the surviving waist protocols (IPv4; TCP and UDP) are old and widely depended on, not necessarily the highest-quality ones.

RFC 1958 (Carpenter, 1996) summarizes the community view: the goal is connectivity, the tool is the Internet Protocol, and the intelligence is end to end rather than hidden in the network; it notes the Internet grew by evolution, not from a grand plan.

The end-to-end argument (Saltzer, Reed, Clark 1984): a function that can be completely and correctly implemented only with knowledge at the endpoints cannot be provided correctly by the communication system alone; low-level versions are justified only as performance enhancements.

The paper's careful-file-transfer example: threats include disk faults, buffering/copy bugs in host software, and host crashes, which per-hop network reliability cannot catch; the robust fix is an end-to-end checksum check and retry. Making each step triple-redundant is judged uneconomical.

Clark (1988) lists the DARPA Internet's goals in priority order: survivability despite loss of networks/gateways; multiple types of service; variety of networks; distributed management; cost effectiveness; low-effort host attachment; accountability. The ordering came from the military context, and the later goals were met least well.
Fate-sharing (Clark 1988): keep connection state at the endpoints, so state is lost only if the entity that cares about it is also lost; gateways can then be stateless datagram switches.

Clark (1988) records that TCP and IP were originally one protocol and were split so that services not wanting reliable byte streams (e.g. packet voice, debugging) could run over IP via UDP — the 'multiple types of service' goal.

In October 1986 the Internet suffered the first of a series of congestion collapses: throughput between LBL and UC Berkeley (sites about 400 yards apart) fell from 32 kb/s to 40 b/s. The fix (slow start, congestion avoidance, better RTT estimation) was placed in end hosts' TCP, not in routers.

RFC 3439 (Bush & Meyer, 2002) names complexity the main barrier to scaling and states a Simplicity Principle, an Amplification Principle (large systems show non-linearities small ones don't; small things can cause huge events) and a Coupling Principle; its section 3 is 'Layering Considered Harmful', warning that stacking layers adds optimization and feature-richness costs.

Cross-layer designs can create unplanned feedback loops and interaction effects that threaten stability, and unstructured cross-layer coupling produces 'spaghetti' architectures that are hard to maintain and that block later innovation.

RFC 7426 separates the forwarding (data) plane, which handles packets per their rules, from the control plane, which decides those rules for one or more devices, and from the management plane, which monitors, configures and maintains devices; it also names an operational plane for a device's overall operating state, and contrasts control vs management by timescale.

Middleboxes constrain protocol evolution: Honda et al. measured paths that rewrite initial sequence numbers, strip or pass unknown TCP options and resegment data, so new TCP extensions (e.g. MPTCP) must be designed to survive them — 'ossification'.
Encrypting transport headers (as QUIC does) helps avoid ossification by middleboxes and hides transport behaviour from the path, at the cost of operator visibility.

RFC 9413 (IAB, 2023) argues that tolerating unexpected input under the robustness principle ('be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept') causes long-term interoperability harm, and recommends active protocol maintenance instead.

Tussle in Cyberspace: stakeholders (users, ISPs, governments, rights holders) have conflicting interests; the architecture should 'design for variation in outcome' — modularize along tussle boundaries and design for choice — rather than dictate one outcome, because rigid designs get broken.

Per-frame overhead for TCP over Ethernet with a 1500-byte MTU: 8 B preamble/SFD + 14 B header + 4 B FCS + 12 B inter-frame gap = 38 B on the wire; IPv4 20 B + TCP 20 B + timestamps 12 B leave 1448 B of payload, so goodput is 1448/1538 ≈ 94.1% of line rate; a 100-byte application message is ≈ 52.6%.

Retry cost arithmetic: with n hops each losing a packet with probability p, end-to-end-only retry succeeds per attempt with probability (1-p)^n and costs on average ((1-(1-p)^n)/p)/(1-p)^n link transmissions, versus n/(1-p) with per-hop retry. n=10,p=1%: 10.6 vs 10.1; n=10,p=10%: 18.7 vs 11.1; n=5,p=30%: 16.5 vs 7.1. This is why lossy links (e.g. Wi-Fi) add link-layer retransmission as a performance enhancement while TCP keeps the end-to-end check.

Availability arithmetic: five components in series at 99.9% each give ≈ 99.50%; two such paths in parallel give ≈ 99.9975% only if their failures are independent — shared fate (same conduit, same software bug, same config push) erases the gain.
Data-plane time budget at 400 Gb/s: a full 1538-byte on-wire frame lasts ≈30.8 ns and a minimum 84-byte on-wire frame ≈1.7 ns, so per-packet work must be fixed-function or pipelined.
Routers police the traffic punted from the data plane to the control-plane CPU (control-plane protection / policing), because flooding that path starves routing protocols.
QUIC connection IDs let a connection survive address changes and let load balancers route without per-connection memory of the 5-tuple.

pitfalls: Reading the end-to-end argument as 'never put function in the network' — the paper explicitly allows in-network versions as performance enhancements; it says they cannot replace the endpoint check.

Treating the OSI 7-layer model as the Internet's architecture; the Internet's working shape is the hourglass around IP, and real systems routinely violate strict layering (NAT, PMTUD, TCP checksum over an IP pseudo-header).
Assuming redundant paths are independent; shared conduits, software and config pushes create correlated failures.
Equating SDN's control/data separation with 'centralization' — the separation is about interfaces; a separated control plane can still be distributed.
Assuming cross-layer optimization is free: it couples layers, creates feedback loops, and freezes the interface it peeks through.

claims.text: A forwarding element's per-packet pipeline is: parse headers, classify/look up (exact, longest-prefix, ternary matches), modify (rewrite MAC, decrement TTL, push/pop labels), then queue and schedule onto the output port; the control plane only fills the tables.
Minimum-size Ethernet frame is 64 B plus 8 B preamble/SFD and 12 B inter-frame gap = 84 B (672 bits) on the wire; at 100 Gb/s that is ~148.8 M packets/s, ~6.7 ns per packet; at 400 Gb/s ~1.68 ns.

Longest-prefix match: an IP destination may match several prefixes; the most specific (longest) wins. The global IPv4 BGP table passed one million prefixes in 2025 (APNIC counted 1,001,332 on 8 May 2025), and the count varies by vantage point.

DIR-24-8 (Gupta, Lin, McKeown 1998): a 2^24-entry first table indexed by the top 24 address bits, plus a second table for longer prefixes; most lookups take one memory access, the rest two; the first table is ~32 MB. DPDK's LPM library uses a variant.

A TCAM stores value+mask per entry and compares the key against every entry in parallel in one cycle; a priority encoder returns the first match, so storing prefixes ordered by length gives longest-prefix match in one access, but inserts may have to move entries to keep the order.

TCAM costs several times more area per bit than SRAM and burns far more power because every search charges every match line; one model gives ~3 µW per bit, and an 18 Mb TCAM at 100–150 MHz is quoted at 10 W or more versus 1–2 W for SRAM.

Exact-match tables (MAC, five-tuple flow tables) are built from hashing into SRAM; ECMP picks among equal-cost next hops by hashing flow fields (hash-threshold in RFC 2992), keeping a flow on one path to avoid reordering at the cost of uneven load when flows differ in size.

With one FIFO per input, head-of-line blocking limits throughput of an N×N input-queued switch under uniform saturated traffic to 2 − √2 ≈ 58.6% as N grows large (Karol, Hluchyj, Morgan 1987); for small N it is higher (0.75 at N=2, ~0.655 at N=4, ~0.618 at N=8).

Virtual output queues (one queue per output at each input) remove HOL blocking; iSLIP, an iterative round-robin matching scheduler, reaches 100% throughput for uniform traffic and never starves a queue; schedulers were built for 32 ports at ~100 M decisions/s.
Pure output queueing needs the output memory to accept up to N packets per slot (N× speedup), which is why high-port-count switches use input/VOQ or shared-memory designs with modest fabric speedup.

Store-and-forward receives the whole frame and checks the FCS before sending, adding one serialization delay per hop (1500 B at 10 Gb/s = 1.2 µs); cut-through starts sending after the header, so latency is roughly independent of frame length, but corrupt frames propagate and cut-through is impossible when the egress is faster than the ingress or the egress is busy.

The buffer rule of thumb is RTT × C; Appenzeller et al. showed a link carrying n long-lived desynchronized TCP flows needs about RTT × C / √n, e.g. a 2.5 Gb/s link with 10,000 flows could cut buffers ~99%; the 2019 Redux paper notes the result changed practice only partly.

RMT (Bosshart et al. 2013): a programmable parser plus 32 physical match-action stages on a 1 GHz pipeline handling 960 M packets/s for 64×10 Gb ports; tables in each stage are built from SRAM (exact match) and TCAM (ternary) blocks; the authors estimate programmability costs ~15% chip area and ~12% power over a fixed-function chip.

P4_16 programs declare headers, a parser state machine, match-action tables with actions, and control blocks that apply tables; the architecture (e.g. v1model, PSA, TNA) fixes what blocks a target exposes. The current spec is v1.2.5 (2024).

Intel announced in January 2023 it would stop developing new Tofino switch ASICs while continuing to sell and support Tofino and Tofino 2; P4 remains used on SmartNICs/DPUs, FPGAs and software targets.
Fixed-function merchant switch ASICs keep doubling: Broadcom's Tomahawk 6 (shipping from June 2025) is a single-chip 102.4 Tb/s switch with up to 512×200G or 1024×100G ports.

SmartNICs/DPUs put programmable packet engines plus general-purpose cores (e.g. NVIDIA BlueField-3: Arm cores, up to 400 Gb/s) on the NIC, so the host's infrastructure work — virtual switching, encryption, storage — runs off the host CPU; AMD Pensando and Intel IPUs are similar parts.

Line-rate hardware is a fixed budget per packet: each pipeline stage gets a fixed number of clock cycles and a fixed number of memory accesses, so programs that need loops, unbounded state or many dependent lookups do not fit; this is why P4 has no loops in the control flow and parsers are bounded state machines.

On 12 August 2014 ('512K day') the IPv4 table briefly passed 512,000 routes after a burst of ~15,000 deaggregated routes; older routers whose default hardware (TCAM) partition held ~512K IPv4 routes overflowed, causing scattered outages, though the vendor had warned beforehand and the fix was a reconfiguration plus reboot.

Packets a hardware parser cannot handle at line rate (e.g. IPv4 options, unusually deep header stacks) are typically punted to a slower CPU path or dropped, which discourages new header formats in the middle of the network.
Broadcom also ships a co-packaged-optics Tomahawk 6 variant (Davisson), moving optical I/O next to the switch die to cut I/O power.
Derived figure: a 102.4 Tb/s chip at 672 bits per minimum-size packet would face ≈1.52×10^11 packets/s if every port ran smallest packets.

The FIB (in the data plane) is not the RIB (in the control plane); a router can hold more routes in software than its hardware tables fit, and overflow means slow-path or dropped traffic.
58.6% is the large-N, uniform, saturated, fixed-cell limit; real HOL loss depends on traffic.

claims.text: Distance-vector routing (distributed Bellman-Ford): each router tells its neighbors its current best distance to every destination and takes min(link cost + neighbor's distance); it never sees the topology.

After a failure, distance-vector can 'count to infinity': routers keep raising their distances via each other's stale reports. RIP caps the metric at 16 = unreachable, limiting the network to 15 hops; it sends full updates every 30 s.

Split horizon: do not advertise a route back out the interface it was learned on; poisoned reverse: advertise it back with metric 16. These fix two-node loops but not every loop of three or more routers under unlucky timing.

Link-state routing: every router floods a description of its own links (LSAs in OSPF, LSPs in IS-IS) to all routers in the area; each builds the same map and runs Dijkstra's shortest-path-first locally.

OSPF runs over IP (protocol 89), uses a two-level hierarchy of areas around a backbone area 0, and areas summarize to bound flooding and SPF cost. IS-IS runs directly over the link layer, not IP, encodes data in extensible TLVs, and uses level-1/level-2 hierarchy; large ISPs often favor IS-IS.

Francois, Filsfils et al. (2005) measured link-state operations on deployed routers and concluded sub-second IGP convergence is achievable in large ISP networks without compromising stability; RIB/FIB update of many prefixes, not SPF itself, tends to dominate.

Path-vector (BGP): advertisements carry the full list of ASes the route has passed (AS_PATH); a router rejects any route containing its own AS, which prevents loops without a global map, and lets each AS apply its own policy.
BGP runs over TCP port 179; it sends incremental UPDATEs (announcements and withdrawals), not periodic full tables.

BGP route selection: first highest LOCAL_PREF (the local 'degree of preference'), then shortest AS_PATH, lowest ORIGIN (IGP<EGP<incomplete), lowest MED (compared by default only among routes from the same neighboring AS), eBGP over iBGP, lowest IGP cost to the next hop, then lowest BGP identifier. Vendors add steps (e.g., Cisco weight before LOCAL_PREF).
iBGP speakers do not re-advertise routes learned from one iBGP peer to another, so plain iBGP needs a full mesh: n routers need n(n-1)/2 sessions (100 routers → 4,950).

Route reflection (RFC 4456): a route reflector re-advertises iBGP routes to its clients; ORIGINATOR_ID records the router that injected the route, CLUSTER_LIST records the reflection path, and both are used to drop looped advertisements. A reflector passes on only its own best path, which hides alternatives from clients.

RFC 3345: with single-level route reflection or confederations and MEDs from two or more neighbor ASes for one prefix, BGP can oscillate persistently; mitigations include deterministic MED ordering and always-compare-MED. It is a case of locally sensible policies conflicting globally.

Gao-Rexford conditions: prefer customer routes over peer/provider routes; export customer routes to everyone but peer/provider routes only to customers; no cycles of provider-customer links. If every AS follows these, BGP is guaranteed to converge. The export rule makes valid paths 'valley-free'.

Labovitz et al. (SIGCOMM 2000) injected faults at exchange points and found BGP took minutes to converge after failures, exploring many temporary paths; the delay comes from path exploration interacting with timers (MinRouteAdvertisementInterval, suggested 30 s for eBGP) and implementation choices.

Route redistribution copies routes between protocols (e.g., BGP or static into OSPF); metrics do not translate, and redistributing in both directions at two points can create routing loops unless tagged and filtered.

RFC 7908 defines a route leak as propagation of routing announcements beyond their intended scope, typically violating the customer/peer/provider export rules (e.g., a customer re-announcing one provider's routes to another).

June 24, 2019: DQE (AS33154) used a BGP optimizer that generated more-specific routes; its customer Allegheny Technologies (AS396531) leaked them to Verizon (AS701), which accepted and propagated them; Cloudflare reported roughly 15% of its global traffic lost at the worst point.

Feb 24, 2008: Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) originated 208.65.153.0/24, a more-specific of YouTube's 208.65.152.0/22; PCCW (AS3491) propagated it and longest-prefix match pulled YouTube traffic worldwide. YouTube countered with /25s; PCCW withdrew AS17557's routes at about 21:01 UTC, around two hours after the start.

RPKI origin validation (RFC 6811): Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) bind a prefix, a maximum length and an origin AS. A route is Valid if a ROA covers it with matching origin and length, Invalid if a ROA covers it but none matches, NotFound if no ROA covers it.

RFC 9319 (BCP 185) recommends avoiding maxLength in ROAs except in specific cases: a loose ROA authorizes unannounced sub-prefixes that a forged-origin attacker (who prepends the real origin AS) can use.
ROV checks only the origin AS; it does not stop a forged path ending in the right origin, or leaks of validly originated routes.
ROA coverage: about 56% of routed IPv4 and 59% of IPv6 address blocks were covered by ROAs as of August 2025.

RFC 9234 (2022) adds BGP Roles negotiated in OPEN (provider, customer, peer, route server, RS client) and the Only to Customer (OTC) attribute (type 35); a route marked OTC must not be sent to a provider or peer, and a marked route arriving from a customer is treated as a leak. BIRD 2.0.11, FRR 8.4 and OpenBGPD 7.5 support it.

ASPA (Autonomous System Provider Authorization) lets an AS sign the list of its providers in the RPKI so receivers can verify the AS_PATH is valley-free and detect leaks and some forged paths; as of late 2026 it is still an Internet-Draft awaiting write-up, not an RFC.

Oct 4, 2021: a maintenance command unintentionally disconnected Facebook's backbone; DNS servers that could no longer reach the data centers withdrew their BGP advertisements by design, making Facebook's names unresolvable for about six hours.
MPLS forwards on short labels pushed by the ingress router; with RSVP-TE, explicit-path tunnels (LSPs) are signaled hop by hop and every router on the path keeps state for every tunnel through it.

Segment Routing (RFC 8402): the ingress puts an ordered list of segments (instructions) in the packet; per-flow state is kept only at the ingress of the SR domain. Prefix segments mean 'go to this node by the IGP shortest path' (ECMP-aware); adjacency segments mean 'leave by this specific link'. SR-MPLS encodes segments as MPLS labels; SRv6 encodes them as IPv6 addresses.
The Internet is made of tens of thousands of autonomous systems (independently administered networks, each with one routing policy and an AS number).
OSPFv2 carries IPv4 only; IPv6 needed a new version, OSPFv3. IS-IS added IPv6, traffic-engineering and segment-routing data as new TLVs.

Mitigations for route reflectors hiding paths include BGP add-path (advertising more than one path) and placing reflectors with the topology in mind; hot-potato routing picks the exit with the lowest IGP cost.

Meta reported that an audit tool meant to block dangerous commands had a bug and did not stop the backbone-disconnecting command; recovery was slowed because internal tools depended on the same network.
Distance-vector computation is the distributed Bellman-Ford algorithm (Bellman 1958, Ford-Fulkerson).

Under RSVP-TE a full mesh of tunnels between n edge routers is n(n-1) unidirectional LSPs (50 edges → 2,450); SR-MPLS core state is roughly one node segment per router plus local adjacency segments, independent of the number of paths. SRv6 segments are 128-bit IPv6 addresses (16 bytes each).

transport-beyond-tcp-basics.fetchNote: Facts gathered via web search snippets of the RFC/draft text and paper abstracts on 2026-11-14 (RFC sites were not fetched directly through the proxy); long-stable textbook facts cross-checked against implementations' comments.

claims.text: TCP's current specification is RFC 9293 (2022), which obsoletes RFC 793; its connection state machine has 11 states (CLOSED, LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT).
The side that closes first waits in TIME-WAIT for 2×MSL so stray old segments die and its final ACK can be resent; busy servers that actively close accumulate TIME-WAIT entries.
Classic loss detection: three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit; otherwise the retransmission timeout (RTO) fires. Reordering by more than three packets is mistaken for loss.

RACK-TLP (RFC 8985) detects loss by time, not by counting duplicate ACKs: a packet is deemed lost if a packet sent sufficiently later has been delivered and a reordering window (a fraction of min RTT, about min_RTT/4, adapted upward when DSACKs show spurious retransmits) has passed. A Tail Loss Probe resends the last segment after ~2 SRTT to turn tail losses into fast recovery instead of an RTO.
Classical PMTUD (RFC 1191) sets Don't Fragment and relies on ICMP 'Packet Too Big' messages; when middleboxes filter ICMP, big packets vanish silently — a PMTU black hole.

Packetization-layer PMTUD (RFC 4821 for TCP, RFC 8899 for datagram transports such as QUIC) probes with larger packets and treats their loss as the signal, so it does not depend on ICMP; RFC 8899 updates RFC 4821.
Mathis et al. (1997): steady-state Reno throughput ≈ (MSS/RTT)·C/√p with C ≈ 1.22 (periodic loss, every packet ACKed); the authors later argued (2019) the model is outdated for modern stacks.

Congestion-control families: loss-based (Reno, CUBIC) reduce on packet loss; delay-based (Vegas, Swift) react to rising RTT; rate/model-based (BBR) estimate bottleneck bandwidth and min RTT and pace; learning-based (Remy offline-optimized rules, PCC Vivace online optimization) search for good actions against a utility function.

CUBIC (RFC 9438, 2023, obsoletes RFC 8312) grows the window as W(t)=C·(t−K)³+W_max with C=0.4 and multiplicative decrease β=0.7; K=∛(W_max(1−β)/C). Growth depends on time since the last loss, not on RTT; a Reno-friendly region keeps it at least as aggressive as Reno with α=3(1−β)/(1+β).
Loss-based control fills whatever buffer sits at the bottleneck before it sees a loss, so a deep buffer turns into standing queueing delay ('bufferbloat').

BBR models the path by two numbers — bottleneck bandwidth (max filter over delivery-rate samples) and round-trip propagation time (min filter over ~10 s) — and aims to keep inflight ≈ BDP. ProbeBW cycles pacing gain (1.25 probe, 0.75 drain, then 1.0 for six rounds in v1); ProbeRTT briefly drops inflight to 4 packets to re-measure min RTT; Startup uses a high gain (2/ln2 ≈ 2.89 in v1).
BBRv3 is specified in the IETF CCWG Internet-Draft draft-ietf-ccwg-bbr (Experimental), adopted as a WG item in 2024 and still a draft in 2026.
BBR (v1) vs CUBIC fairness depends on buffer depth: BBR takes more bandwidth when buffers are shallow despite high loss, CUBIC does better when buffers are deep.

DCTCP (RFC 8257): switches ECN-mark when the instantaneous queue exceeds a threshold K; the sender keeps α ← (1−g)α + g·F with F the fraction of marked bytes per window (g = 1/16 typical) and cuts cwnd ← cwnd·(1−α/2) at most once per window. The SIGCOMM paper suggests K > C·RTT/7 and used K ≈ 65 packets at 10 Gb/s.

RFC 8257 says DCTCP is for controlled environments such as data centers and must not be deployed over the public Internet without additional measures, because it reacts to ECN differently from standard TCP (RFC 3168).

Swift (Google, SIGCOMM 2020) is delay-based AIMD toward a target delay using NIC hardware timestamps, keeping separate fabric and endpoint windows and using the minimum; deployed in Google data centers for years.

Learning-based congestion control remains largely research: Remy computes rules offline for an assumed range of networks; PCC Vivace adjusts rate online by measuring a utility of throughput, latency and loss. Surveys call the field immature, and performance outside the trained conditions is a known risk.

QUIC (RFC 9000) runs over UDP, implements streams, flow control, loss recovery and congestion control in user space, and integrates TLS 1.3 (RFC 9001); almost all of its header beyond a few bits, the connection ID and the packet number field is encrypted, and the packet number itself is header-protected.
QUIC streams are independent: a lost packet only stalls the streams whose data it carried, removing TCP's cross-stream head-of-line blocking for multiplexed HTTP (HTTP/3).

RFC 9002: QUIC packet numbers increase monotonically and are never reused, so retransmitted data goes in a new packet and the 'which copy was ACKed?' ambiguity disappears; ACK frames carry the ACK delay; loss is declared after a packet threshold of 3 or a time threshold of 9/8 × max(smoothed RTT, latest RTT); the default congestion controller resembles NewReno, but implementations commonly use CUBIC or BBR.
QUIC's initial window per RFC 9002 is min(10·max_datagram_size, max(14720 bytes, 2·max_datagram_size)).

A fresh TCP+TLS 1.3 connection needs 2 RTTs before the first request is sent with data (1 for TCP, 1 for TLS); QUIC combines them into 1 RTT, and with a resumption ticket can send 0-RTT data in the first flight.

0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker and has weaker forward secrecy; it must not carry non-idempotent requests. HTTP's RFC 8470 defines the Early-Data header and 425 (Too Early) status for servers to refuse risky early requests.

QUIC connections are identified by connection IDs, not the address 4-tuple, so a client can migrate (e.g. Wi-Fi to cellular); the peer must validate the new path with PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE before sending much there, and endpoints switch to fresh connection IDs to resist linking across paths.

Langley et al. (2017) reported QUIC at ~7% of Internet traffic and over 30% of Google's egress at the time; it was built in user space partly so it could evolve faster than kernel TCP and avoid middlebox ossification.

MPTCP v1 (RFC 8684, 2020, obsoletes RFC 6824) spreads one connection over several TCP subflows; the first subflow negotiates with MP_CAPABLE (exchanging keys), later subflows join with MP_JOIN authenticated by those keys; a data-sequence mapping reassembles the byte stream across subflows.

Coupled congestion control (RFC 6356, LIA) links the subflows' window increases so a multipath flow takes no more than a single-path TCP would on the best path at a shared bottleneck, while moving traffic away from congested paths.
Apple's iOS 7 (2013) used MPTCP for Siri — the first large-scale commercial deployment — so a session survived moving from Wi-Fi to cellular.

Wireless links lose packets to fading and interference, not only to congestion; loss-based control misreads those losses, so Wi-Fi and cellular do link-layer retransmission, which in turn adds variable delay and large buffers (cellular bufferbloat).
TCP's window field is 16 bits (64 KB max); the window-scale option negotiated in the SYN multiplies it (up to ~1 GB), which long, fast paths need because throughput ≤ window / RTT.
VXLAN encapsulation adds 50 bytes over IPv4 (outer Ethernet 14 + IP 20 + UDP 8 + VXLAN 8), so a 1500-byte underlay cannot carry 1500-byte inner packets without fragmentation or a larger underlay MTU.

Encrypting transport headers removes signals operators used to measure RTT and loss passively; QUIC defines a single optional 'spin bit' that endpoints may flip once per round trip as a voluntary latency signal.
CUBIC is the default congestion controller in the Linux, Windows and Apple TCP stacks.
Later BBR versions (v2, v3) use loss and ECN as signals alongside the bandwidth/RTT model, addressing v1's disregard of loss.
Measurements found many Internet paths strip, rewrite or block unknown TCP options, which is why new transport features are hard to deploy in TCP.
Worked: at 10 Gb/s and 100 ms a 1460-byte-MSS Reno flow needs a window of ~86,000 segments; after one halving, +1 per RTT takes ~43,000 RTTs ≈ 70 min to recover.

pitfalls: Treating three duplicate ACKs as proof of loss — multipath fabrics and wireless links reorder; RACK's time window is the modern fix.

congestion-scheduling-qos.fetchNote: Facts from web search snippets of RFC/draft text, papers and implementation docs on 2026-11-14; long-stable queueing-theory results from the textbook. Queue numbers reuse NetViz.queue / NetViz.md1 (M/D/1) so they agree with chapters 02 and 04.

claims.text: A queue forms whenever packets arrive faster than the link drains them, even briefly; delay = waiting + service, jitter is the variation of that delay, loss happens when the buffer is full (drop-tail).
Little's law: mean number in a system = arrival rate × mean time in the system (L = λW), for any stable queue regardless of arrival or service distribution.

For random (Poisson) arrivals and fixed service time (M/D/1), mean number in system = ρ + ρ²/(2(1−ρ)) and mean time in system = 1 + ρ/(2(1−ρ)) service times; at ρ = 0.5, 0.8, 0.95 the mean time is 1.5, 3, 10.5 service times. For M/M/1 mean time = 1/(1−ρ). Delay grows without bound as load → 1.
A 1,500-byte packet takes 1.2 ms to serialize at 10 Mb/s, 120 µs at 100 Mb/s, 1.2 µs at 10 Gb/s; a full buffer of B bytes on a link of rate C adds B/C of delay to every packet behind it.
Buffer sizing: the classic rule is one bandwidth-delay product; Appenzeller et al. (2004) argued BDP/√n suffices with n desynchronized long flows (covered in chapter 02).

Drop-tail FIFO with large buffers produces standing queues under loss-based TCP (bufferbloat) and synchronizes flows' backoffs; RFC 7567 (BCP 197, 2015, replacing RFC 2309) strongly recommends deploying AQM but no longer recommends RED specifically.

RED (Floyd & Jacobson 1993) keeps an exponentially weighted average queue length; below min_th it never drops, between min_th and max_th it drops/marks with probability rising linearly to max_p, above max_th it drops all; the paper suggests a small averaging weight (w_q = 0.002). RED's sensitivity to parameter choice limited its deployment.

ECN (RFC 3168) uses the two low bits of the old IPv4 TOS / IPv6 Traffic Class byte: 00 Not-ECT, 10 ECT(0), 01 ECT(1), 11 CE. An AQM can set CE instead of dropping on ECN-capable packets; the receiver echoes it (ECE flag in TCP) and the sender reacts as if to a loss and sets CWR.

CoDel (Nichols & Jacobson 2012; RFC 8289, Experimental, 2018) timestamps packets on enqueue and measures sojourn time at dequeue; if the minimum sojourn time stays above target (default 5 ms) for at least an interval (default 100 ms), it enters a dropping state and spaces drops by interval/√count, so the drop rate rises until the queue drains. It ignores good queues (bursts that drain within an interval) and needs no tuning to link rate.

FQ-CoDel (RFC 8290, Experimental, 2018) hashes packets into flow queues (Linux default 1024), serves them with deficit round robin using a byte quantum (default 1514 bytes, an Ethernet MTU-sized frame), keeps separate 'new' and 'old' flow lists so sparse flows (that have not built a queue) are served first, and runs CoDel independently on each flow queue. It is the default qdisc in many Linux distributions (via systemd) and in OpenWrt.
FIFO gives no isolation: one aggressive flow's queue delays everyone. Strict priority gives the high class minimal delay but can starve lower classes unless the high class is rate-limited.

Fair queueing (Demers, Keshav, Shenker 1989) approximates bit-by-bit round robin by computing a virtual finish time per packet and sending the smallest; weighted fair queueing gives each flow a share proportional to its weight. Parekh & Gallager (1993) showed that with WFQ (PGPS) a token-bucket-constrained flow (burst σ, rate ρ) guaranteed rate g ≥ ρ at a single node has worst-case delay ≤ σ/g + L_max/g + L_max/C (L_max the largest packet, C the link rate), whatever other flows do.

Classic WFQ needs O(log n) work per packet to keep finish times sorted; Deficit Round Robin (Shreedhar & Varghese, 1995) is O(1): each active queue gets a quantum of bytes per round added to a deficit counter, sends packets while the head packet fits in the counter, and carries leftover credit; it is fair in throughput but gives weaker latency bounds than WFQ.

Hierarchical scheduling (e.g. Linux HTB) arranges classes in a tree: each class has a guaranteed rate and a ceiling, and leaf classes borrow unused bandwidth from their parent, so an operator can split a link among customers and then among each customer's applications.
A token bucket (rate r, depth b) bounds traffic: over any interval t, at most b + r·t bytes pass. Policers drop or re-mark excess; shapers delay it in a queue.

DiffServ (RFC 2474/2475) redefines the IPv4 TOS / IPv6 Traffic Class byte as a 6-bit DS field (DSCP) plus 2 ECN bits. Edge routers classify, meter, police and mark; core routers only look at the DSCP and apply a per-hop behavior (PHB) — no per-flow state in the core.

Expedited Forwarding (RFC 3246, DSCP 46) is a low-delay, low-jitter, low-loss PHB: EF traffic must be served at least at a configured rate, and it must be policed at the edge so it cannot starve others. Assured Forwarding (RFC 2597) has 4 classes × 3 drop precedences, AFxy with DSCP = 8x + 2y (AF11 = 10 … AF43 = 38); it gives no strict bandwidth guarantee per packet. Default/best effort is DSCP 0; Class Selector CSx = 8x keeps compatibility with old IP Precedence.

RFC 4594 is Informational: it recommends service classes and DSCPs (e.g. telephony EF, multimedia conferencing AF4x, network control CS6) but networks are free to use their own mappings; DSCPs have only local meaning between domains unless agreed.

Measurement (Secchi, Fairhurst, Custura et al. 2018, ~25,000 path pairs) found some form of DSCP modification on over 70% of sampled Internet paths, including bleaching to zero and remarking that can cause priority inversion; end-to-end DSCP across the public Internet cannot be relied on.
RFC 8325 (2018) maps DSCPs to IEEE 802.11 User Priority, and so to the four WMM access categories (voice, video, best effort, background), which contend for airtime with different backoff parameters.

IntServ (RFC 1633) offers per-flow Guaranteed and Controlled-Load services; RSVP (RFC 2205) sets up reservations with PATH messages downstream and RESV messages upstream from receivers, as soft state that must be refreshed (default every 30 s). RFC 2208 (1997) warned that router state and processing grow with the number of reservations and that backbones would likely not run per-flow RSVP; IntServ/RSVP never deployed at Internet scale.

RSVP survives as RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) for signalling MPLS traffic-engineering tunnels: reservations are per tunnel (aggregate), not per application flow, and the tunnel's bandwidth is control-plane bookkeeping — the data plane does not police it unless configured.

ITU-T G.114 recommends one-way delay below 150 ms for most interactive voice; voice apps use a jitter buffer that trades added delay for smoothness, so jitter turns into delay or into late (lost) packets.

L4S (RFCs 9330–9332, Jan 2023) marks packets ECT(1) to request a shallow-queue service; a Dual-Queue Coupled AQM keeps an L4S queue with ~1 ms marking threshold next to a classic queue and couples their signals so scalable (DCTCP/Prague-like) and classic (CUBIC/Reno) flows share capacity roughly fairly; the L4S marking probability is k (=2) times the square root of the classic drop probability.

After field trials from mid-2023, Comcast began rolling out L4S-based low-latency DOCSIS in January 2025 in several US markets (Atlanta, Chicago, Colorado Springs, Philadelphia, Rockville, San Francisco), with Apple FaceTime, NVIDIA GeForce NOW, Meta and Valve as launch apps; Apple had L4S support since iOS 17/macOS Sonoma.
DCTCP-style data-center transport pairs a shallow ECN marking threshold in switches with proportional sender response (covered in chapter 04).
CAKE (2018) builds on FQ-CoDel for home gateways, adding a built-in shaper so the queue can be moved from the modem into the router, plus per-host fairness.

CoDel does not drop when the queue holds less than about one MTU of bytes, since a single packet's own transmission time can exceed the target on slow links; on very slow links the target should be at least one packet's transmission time.

pitfalls: Utilization near 100% looks efficient but delay explodes: M/D/1 at 95% load is 10.5 service times mean, and the tail is far worse.
Bigger buffers do not reduce loss for loss-based TCP; they add standing delay (bufferbloat).
AQM only helps at the queue that actually builds — usually the access uplink or Wi-Fi, not the core; a shaper placed just below the bottleneck rate moves the queue to where FQ-CoDel can manage it.
Strict priority without a policer lets a mis-marked or runaway class starve everything else.
DSCP markings set by hosts are routinely bleached or remarked at domain boundaries; trust and re-mark at the edge.
QoS cannot create capacity: it only chooses who waits when the link is full; prioritising more than a small share of traffic as 'high' makes it ordinary again.
MPLS-TE bandwidth reservations are bookkeeping in the control plane; real traffic can exceed them unless policed.
DRR with a quantum smaller than the largest packet needs several rounds before that packet goes; FQ-CoDel's quantum is set to one MTU-sized frame for this reason.
A shaper set slightly below the real bottleneck rate (e.g. 95%) moves the queue into a device that runs FQ-CoDel/CAKE; without it the queue stays in an unmanaged modem FIFO.

network-security-and-trust.fetchNote: Primary RFC hosts were not fetched directly; RFC facts are long-stable protocol knowledge cross-checked against search snippets of RFC text, vendor docs and incident reports. Volatile numbers (attack records, PQ adoption, DNSSEC validation) come from 2025-2026 reporting.

claims.text: A threat model names who the attacker is, where they sit and what they can do. An on-path (man-in-the-middle) attacker can read, drop, change and inject packets on the path; an off-path attacker cannot see traffic and must guess values (ports, sequence numbers, IDs) to inject; an insider already holds valid credentials or a foothold inside.

TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446): a full handshake takes one round trip; key exchange is always ephemeral (EC)DHE, so it has forward secrecy; static-RSA key transport, renegotiation and non-AEAD ciphers were removed; everything after ServerHello, including the server certificate, is encrypted.

In TLS the server proves its identity by signing the handshake transcript (CertificateVerify) with the key in its certificate; the certificate chain is trusted because a CA in the client's root store signed it. Encryption without that check gives secrecy only against passive listeners, not against an on-path attacker.

DigiNotar (2011): an intruder issued a fraudulent *.google.com certificate (dated 10 July 2011) used to intercept Gmail users, mainly in Iran; Fox-IT counted about 300,000 unique requesting IPs. Chrome's pinned keys for Google flagged it. Browsers removed DigiNotar from their trust stores and the company went bankrupt. Any one trusted CA can vouch for any name.

Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962; v2 RFC 9162) puts issued certificates in public append-only Merkle-tree logs; browsers require signed certificate timestamps, so a mis-issued certificate becomes visible to domain owners who watch the logs. It detects, it does not prevent.

CA/Browser Forum Ballot SC-081v3 (passed April 2025) cuts public TLS certificate lifetimes from 398 days to 200 days (15 March 2026), 100 days (15 March 2027) and 47 days (15 March 2029); domain-validation reuse shrinks to 10 days by 2029. Short lives limit how long a stolen key stays useful and push automation.

Hybrid post-quantum key exchange X25519MLKEM768 (X25519 + ML-KEM-768) is on by default in Chrome (since 131, Nov 2024) and Firefox; Cloudflare reported over half of human HTTPS traffic using post-quantum key agreement by late October 2025. It defends against record-now-decrypt-later; certificates and signatures are still classical.

SSH (RFC 4253): the client authenticates the server by its host key, normally trust-on-first-use (known_hosts) unless keys are distributed or signed by an SSH CA; key exchange is ephemeral. OpenSSH 9.0 (2022) made sntrup761x25519-sha512 the default and OpenSSH 10.0 (April 2025) switched the default to hybrid mlkem768x25519-sha256.

IPsec splits into IKEv2 (RFC 7296, key negotiation and mutual authentication, UDP 500, moving to UDP 4500 when NAT is detected) and ESP (RFC 4303, encrypted+authenticated payload with a 32-bit SPI, a sequence number and an anti-replay window). Transport mode protects the payload and keeps the original IP header; tunnel mode wraps the whole packet in a new outer header (site-to-site VPNs).

WireGuard fixes one cipher suite (Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2s) with no negotiation, uses a Noise IK handshake of one round trip, identifies peers by static public keys, and stays silent to unauthenticated packets; its 'cryptokey routing' binds each allowed source prefix to one peer key.

DNSSEC (RFC 4033-4035) signs DNS data: RRSIG records carry signatures, DNSKEY holds zone keys, DS in the parent vouches for the child's key, building a chain up to the root's key-signing key. It gives origin authentication and integrity, not confidentiality; authenticated denial uses NSEC/NSEC3.

The root KSK rolled from KSK-2017 to KSK-2024 (key tag 38696): KSK-2024 published in the root zone on 11 January 2025, the root signed only with KSK-2024 from 11 October 2026, and KSK-2017 is scheduled for revocation on 11 January 2027.
APNIC measurement (October 2026) estimated about 1.7 billion of 4.3 billion users (≈39%) sit behind DNSSEC-validating resolvers; signing of domains lags far behind validation.

DNS transaction IDs are 16 bits. Kaminsky (2008) showed an off-path attacker can trigger endless queries for random non-existent names and race forged answers carrying a malicious delegation, so one hit poisons a whole zone in the cache. The fix — randomizing UDP source ports (RFC 5452) — adds roughly 16 more bits; it raises cost, it does not authenticate answers.

SAD DNS (2020) used a side channel in Linux's global ICMP rate limit to learn a resolver's open source port, then guessed only the 16-bit ID — undoing port randomization. Only cryptographic authentication (DNSSEC) closes the class.

DNS over TLS (RFC 7858, port 853) and DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484) encrypt the client-to-resolver hop, hiding queries from on-path watchers; they say nothing about whether the resolver's answer is true — that is DNSSEC's job.
BCP 38 (RFC 2827, 2000) asks every network to drop packets leaving it whose source address is not its own; deployment remains incomplete, so source-spoofing reflection attacks remain possible.

Reflection-amplification: the attacker sends small UDP requests with the victim's spoofed source address to open servers whose replies are larger. US-CERT TA14-017A lists bandwidth amplification factors such as DNS 28-54, NTP (monlist) 556.9 and memcached 10,000-51,000.

On 28 February 2018 GitHub received a memcached-amplified attack peaking at 1.35 Tb/s; it moved traffic to Akamai's scrubbing service after about 10 minutes, and the site was intermittently unavailable for under 10 minutes in total.

Mirai (2016) built a botnet from IoT devices still using factory-default telnet credentials (about 62 username/password pairs); it hit Krebs on Security at about 620 Gb/s and the DNS provider Dyn on 21 October 2016, making many large sites unreachable.

HTTP/2 Rapid Reset (CVE-2023-44487, Aug-Oct 2023): clients open a stream and cancel it at once with RST_STREAM, so the concurrent-stream limit never binds; Cloudflare saw a peak of just over 201 million requests/s, Google 398 million, AWS 155 million.

Volumetric records rose through 2025: Cloudflare reported 7.3 Tb/s (May), 11.5 and 22.2 Tb/s (September), 29.7 Tb/s and then 31.4 Tb/s (November 2025, about 35 seconds long), all mitigated automatically; botnets of compromised devices (Aisuru) were blamed.
SYN floods exhaust a server's half-open connection table; SYN cookies (RFC 4987) encode the connection state into the server's initial sequence number so no state is kept until the final ACK returns.

Operators push DDoS defences into routing: remotely triggered black-holing (the BLACKHOLE community 65535:666, RFC 7999) asks upstreams to drop all traffic to a target prefix — which completes the attack for that address but saves the rest; BGP Flowspec (RFC 8955) distributes finer match-and-drop/rate-limit rules. Scrubbing centres attract the prefix (BGP or DNS) and return cleaned traffic via tunnels.

NAT (RFC 4787 behaviours) blocks unsolicited inbound connections only as a side effect of keeping per-flow mapping state; it is not a security policy, and endpoint-independent mappings plus port prediction let peers punch through.

Zero trust (NIST SP 800-207, 2020): no implicit trust from network location; access to each resource is granted per session by a policy decision point using identity, device health and context, enforced at a policy enforcement point; all communication is secured regardless of location. Google's BeyondCorp (2014 onward) moved employee access from the VPN-plus-perimeter model to per-request device and user checks.

Microsegmentation applies allow-lists between workloads (east-west), not only at the perimeter, so a compromised host can reach only the few services its role needs; this caps an intruder's lateral movement.

Edge security appliances are themselves attack surface: Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2023-46805 (auth bypass) chained with CVE-2024-21887 (command injection) gave unauthenticated remote code execution, exploited from December 2023; CISA Emergency Directive 24-01 ordered US federal agencies to act, later to disconnect the appliances by 2 February 2024.

XZ Utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094): a contributor who spent about two years earning co-maintainer trust added code to the 5.6.0/5.6.1 release tarballs (not the git tree) that hooked into sshd via liblzma on some Linux distributions, enabling authentication bypass for the attacker's key; Andres Freund, a PostgreSQL developer, found it on 29 March 2024 after noticing sshd logins used ~500 ms extra CPU.

Configuration is a security property: the 2019 Verizon/DQE route leak and Meta's 2021 outage (both in the routing chapter) show one bad change propagating Internet-wide; RPKI ROV and RFC 9234 roles are protocol-level checks on mistakes and attacks alike.
After the 2018 memcached attacks, memcached 1.5.6 disabled its UDP listener by default.

CA/Browser Forum Ballot SC-067 requires CAs to perform domain-control validation from multiple network perspectives (phased in from 2025), so a single local BGP or DNS hijack is less likely to fool validation.
Browser and OS root programs each include many dozens of root CAs, any of which may issue for any domain name unless constrained (e.g., by CAA records).

pitfalls: Treating NAT as a firewall: it blocks unsolicited inbound only as a side effect, and IPv6 deployments often have no NAT.
Encryption without authentication (accepting any certificate, ignoring SSH host-key warnings) protects only against passive listeners.
DoH/DoT hide queries but do not prove answers are genuine; DNSSEC proves answers but does not hide them.
RPKI ROV checks only origin AS; forged-origin paths and leaks of valid routes pass.
Black-holing a victim prefix stops collateral damage but finishes the attacker's job for that address.
The VPN concentrator or firewall is itself internet-facing code; perimeter boxes have been a leading initial-access vector.
Zero trust is an architecture and set of tenets, not a product you buy; a VPN with MFA is still location-based trust once inside.
0-RTT data in TLS 1.3/QUIC is replayable; keep it to idempotent requests.

sdn-and-programmability.fetchNote: Direct page fetches were refused by the agent proxy during this pass; claims below were verified from search-result excerpts of the primary sources (paper abstracts/introductions, RFC text, official incident report). Exact numbers not confirmed from primary text (e.g. controller-placement latencies in ms) were deliberately left out.

claims.text: RFC 7426 splits a network element into a forwarding plane, control plane, management plane (and an operational plane), with southbound abstraction layers between them and northbound interfaces up to applications; SDN is defined by what is moved off the box and how the layers talk, not by a product.

OpenFlow (McKeown et al., CCR April 2008) gives an Ethernet switch an internal flow table and a standardized interface to add and remove flow entries; each entry has an action, and a remote controller programs the table over a secure channel. Its stated goal was to let researchers run experiments on production campus networks.

OpenFlow's fixed set of matchable header fields grew from 12 in version 1.0 (2009) to 41 in version 1.4 (2013); the P4 paper used this growth to argue the switch should instead be told how to parse and match.

P4 (Bosshart et al., 2014) has three goals: reconfigurability in the field, protocol independence (the switch is not tied to any packet format; the program declares headers and a parser), and target independence (a compiler maps the program to a given target).

P4Runtime is a gRPC API from the control plane to a P4 target: SetForwardingPipelineConfig installs a compiled pipeline; Write/Read install and read table entries; a long-lived StreamChannel carries packet-in/packet-out and mastership arbitration. Controllers send a MasterArbitrationUpdate with an election_id per (device_id, role); the highest election_id becomes primary and only the primary may write.

NETCONF (RFC 6241) is an RPC protocol for configuration with distinct datastores (running, optionally candidate and startup), <edit-config>, <lock>, <commit>, and confirmed commit: a confirmed commit is rolled back automatically unless a confirming commit arrives within the timeout (default 600 seconds) or if the session drops.

YANG (RFC 7950, version 1.1) is the data-modelling language that describes the configuration and state trees NETCONF, RESTCONF (RFC 8040, HTTP-based) and gNMI carry; OpenConfig publishes vendor-neutral YANG models.

gNMI is a gRPC service with four RPCs: Capabilities, Get, Set and Subscribe. Subscribe modes are ONCE, POLL and STREAM; STREAM subscriptions are SAMPLE (every interval), ON_CHANGE (only when the value changes) or TARGET_DEFINED.

RFC 9315 (IRTF, Informational, Oct 2022) defines an intent-based network as one that can be managed using intent, and splits the function into intent fulfillment (ingestion, translation, orchestration) and intent assurance (monitoring, compliance assessment, compliance actions); it notes the term is used loosely and distinguishes intent from policy and service models.

The controller placement problem (Heller, Sherwood, McKeown 2012) frames placement as minimum k-median (average latency) or minimum k-center (worst-case latency) over the topology; across 100+ WAN topologies, one controller location is often enough for latency in smaller networks, a few suffice for most, adding more gives diminishing returns, and placement is then driven by fault tolerance and load.

Per-packet consistent update (Reitblatt et al., SIGCOMM 2012): every packet is handled entirely by the old configuration or entirely by the new, never a mix. The general mechanism is a two-phase update: install the new rules (matching a new version tag) in the core while the old ones stay, then flip ingress switches to stamp packets with the new version, then remove old rules. Cost: roughly double rule-table space during the update and slower updates on memory-limited switches.

B4 (Google, SIGCOMM 2013) is a private WAN between Google data centers built with OpenFlow-controlled switches and centralized traffic engineering; many links run near 100% utilization and all links average about 70% over long periods, versus the conventional 30–40% average provisioning — a 2–3× efficiency gain.

B4's control is layered: at each site an OpenFlow controller cluster uses Paxos to elect a master with hot standbys; routing (BGP/IS-IS via Quagga) runs on site servers alongside; a global layer (SDN gateway, central TE server) sits above. TE is layered on the baseline shortest-path routing, so operators could disable TE and fall back to shortest-path forwarding, which the authors called invaluable.

SWAN (Microsoft, SIGCOMM 2013) centrally controls how much each service sends and reconfigures the data plane frequently; it keeps a small amount of scratch capacity on links so that updates are provably congestion-free regardless of the order and timing of switch updates, and carried about 60% more traffic than prior practice in testbed/simulation.

Orion (NSDI 2021) is Google's second-generation SDN control plane for Jupiter data-center fabrics, campus and B4: micro-service applications coordinate through a publish-subscribe Network Information Base (NIB); intent flows down and controllers continually reconcile intent with observed state; the paper reports up to 40× faster convergence and up to 1.16 million network updates per second.

Google Cloud incident 19009 (2 June 2019): a maintenance automation descheduled network control-plane jobs in multiple locations because their clusters were wrongly eligible for a rare maintenance event; the data plane kept forwarding on its last programmed state ('fail static') for several minutes, then capacity was lost, causing 3h19m–4h25m of elevated packet loss across several US regions. Recovery was slow because configuration had to be rebuilt; fixes included persisting control-plane config and failing static for longer.

Header Space Analysis (NSDI 2012) models a header as an L-bit string with no fixed field meanings and each box as a function on that space, so reachability, loops and isolation can be checked statically and protocol-independently. VeriFlow (NSDI 2013) sits between controller and switches and checks network-wide invariants as each rule is inserted, modified or deleted, in real time.

Batfish (NSDI 2015) derives the data plane directly from router configurations (originally by translating them to a Datalog variant), so a config change can be checked for reachability and policy violations before it is pushed; the later tool dropped Datalog.

In-band Network Telemetry (P4.org INT v2.1, 2020) defines modes INT-XD (each node exports data directly), INT-MX (the source embeds instructions; nodes export) and INT-MD (each hop embeds its own metadata, e.g. its queue and latency readings, into the packet); a sink strips it and reports to a collector.

Control-plane separation shares Sheet 01's planes vocabulary and Sheet 02's programmable match-action pipelines (RMT, P4): SDN changes who fills the tables; programmable data planes change what tables exist.

The 2008 OpenFlow paper lists three basic actions for a flow entry: forward the flow's packets to given port(s), encapsulate and send them to the controller (typically a new flow's first packet, so the controller can decide and install an entry), or drop them; every entry also keeps counters.

Derived: light in optical fibre travels about 2×10^8 m/s, ≈5 µs per km, so a controller 4,000 km away adds ≈20 ms one way and ≈40 ms per round trip before any processing — the reason WAN controllers install rules ahead of time (proactively) rather than per new flow.

Derived (standard majority-quorum arithmetic, as used by Paxos/Raft-style leader election): 2f+1 replicas tolerate f failures — 3 survive 1, 5 survive 2; an even count adds no tolerance (4 still survives only 1).
Derived from B4's figures: carrying the same traffic at ~70% average utilization instead of ~35% needs about half the link capacity.

pitfalls: 'SDN = OpenFlow' — OpenFlow is one southbound protocol; most production SDN (B4, Orion, cloud fabrics) mixes OpenFlow/P4Runtime with BGP, gNMI and custom APIs; the architectural move is logically centralized control, not a wire format.

'Logically centralized' is not 'one server': controllers are replicated (Paxos/Raft-style leader election) and often sharded; the hard part is consistency between replicas and between the controller's view and the switches.

Updating switches one by one in any order can create transient loops, black holes or congestion even when old and new configurations are both correct; this needs ordering, version-tagged two-phase updates, or scratch capacity.

A controller that cannot reach a switch is not a data-plane failure; 'fail static' keeps forwarding on the last state, but for how long, and what happens when the state ages out, must be designed (Google 2019).
Intent-based networking is often marketing; RFC 9315's useful test is whether the system both translates intent and continuously assures it.
Automation multiplies mistakes as well as fixes: a wrong change pushed by software reaches every box at once, so verification and staged rollout matter more, not less.

virtualization-overlays-cloud.fetchNote: Direct page fetches were not used; claims verified from search-result excerpts of RFC text, paper abstracts and official docs. Header sizes are standard field arithmetic. Hyperplane internals (third-party notes only) deliberately left out.

claims.text: An 802.1Q VLAN tag is 4 bytes and carries a 12-bit VLAN ID: 4096 values, of which 0 and 4095 are reserved, leaving 4094 usable VLANs. 802.1ad (QinQ) stacks a provider tag (EtherType 0x88A8) outside the customer tag, giving up to 4094 x 4094 combinations.

GRE (RFC 2784) has a 4-byte base header (flags/version + protocol type); RFC 2890 adds optional 4-byte Key and Sequence Number fields. GRE over IPv4 therefore adds 24 bytes (20 outer IP + 4 GRE) to an inner IP packet.

VXLAN (RFC 7348) wraps a whole Ethernet frame in UDP/IP with an 8-byte VXLAN header carrying a 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier (~16 million segments). The IANA destination port is UDP 4789; Linux historically defaulted to 8472 for backward compatibility.
VXLAN over IPv4 adds 50 bytes to the inner IP packet (14 inner Ethernet + 8 VXLAN + 8 UDP + 20 outer IPv4); over IPv6 it adds 70. With a 1500-byte underlay MTU the inner IP MTU is 1450 (IPv4 outer).

RFC 7348 recommends the VTEP compute the outer UDP source port from a hash of inner-packet fields, so underlay ECMP and LAG hashing spread different inner flows across paths while keeping one flow on one path; the outer UDP checksum is usually sent as zero over IPv4.

RFC 7348 VXLAN defines no control plane: it relies on flood-and-learn, with unknown/broadcast traffic sent to an IP multicast group per VNI and MAC-to-VTEP mappings learned from received packets. It provides no authentication or encryption.

EVPN (RFC 7432) uses MP-BGP to advertise MAC/IP reachability; RFC 8365 (2018) applies it as the control plane for overlays over IP, including VXLAN, NVGRE and MPLS-over-GRE, with multihoming procedures (split-horizon, mass withdrawal).

Geneve (RFC 8926, Proposed Standard, Nov 2020) uses UDP port 6081, a 24-bit VNI, and variable-length type-length-value options (Opt Len in 4-byte units); a Critical bit means a receiver that does not understand the option must drop the packet. The base header is 8 bytes, so base overhead matches VXLAN.

RFC 9638 (NVO3 encapsulation considerations, 2024) notes that variable-length headers and options raise hardware-efficiency concerns, and that Geneve was selected assuming the header would typically be parsed in software on a server.

Tunnels in the middle of a network reduce the effective MTU; if outer packets need fragmentation and ICMP "packet too big" is filtered, large packets silently vanish (PMTUD black hole). Options are a larger underlay MTU, a smaller inner MTU, TCP MSS clamping, or packetization-layer PMTUD.

Google Andromeda (NSDI 2018) is GCP's network virtualization stack: a hierarchical control plane plus a fast on-host software switch. Its Hoverboard model sends low-bandwidth long-tail flows through gateways by default and installs direct host-to-host flows only for heavy flows, letting the control plane program connectivity for tens of thousands of VMs in seconds.

Open vSwitch (NSDI 2015) caches forwarding decisions in the kernel: a microflow cache in front of a megaflow cache whose wildcard entries collapse all relevant OpenFlow tables; a 24-hour dataset from 1,000 hypervisors showed median cache size under 107 entries and 7,033 at the 99th percentile.

Azure VFP (NSDI 2017) is the host virtual switch implementing tenant policy (tunneling, ACLs, load balancing). AccelNet (NSDI 2018) offloads VFP's data plane to FPGA SmartNICs, deployed on all new Azure servers since late 2015 in a fleet of over 1M hosts, reporting under 15 microseconds VM-to-VM TCP latency and 32 Gb/s; the control plane stays in software.

Maglev (NSDI 2016) is Google's software network load balancer on commodity Linux servers: routers spread packets across Maglev machines with ECMP; each uses consistent hashing plus connection tracking so a backend change or Maglev failure disturbs few connections. A single machine can saturate 10 Gb/s with small packets; it served Google traffic since 2008.

kube-proxy in iptables mode evaluates rule chains whose length grows with services and endpoints; Cilium replaces it with eBPF programs that look services up in eBPF hash maps, with optional XDP acceleration and Maglev hashing.

The NFV white paper (October 2012, written by network operators, presented in Darmstadt) proposed running network functions such as firewalls, load balancers and gateways as software on standard servers and led to the ETSI NFV industry specification group; it states NFV and SDN are complementary but independent.
Service chaining steers traffic through an ordered list of functions; the Network Service Header (RFC 8300) carries a service path identifier and index plus metadata between them.

In AWS, instances in a VPC support 9001-byte jumbo frames, but traffic through an internet gateway, over VPN, or between regions (without a transit gateway) is limited to 1500 bytes. VPC peering cannot be created between VPCs with overlapping CIDR blocks.

A widely-reported Calico issue: with VXLAN tx-checksum offload on Linux kernels below 5.7, pod-to-Service connections (where some wrapped UDP packets left with bad checksums and were discarded) saw ~63-second delays; Calico now disables VXLAN offload by default. 63 s is the cumulative time of TCP SYN retransmissions starting at a 1 s RTO and doubling (1+2+4+8+16+32), so a connection that succeeds on the sixth retry waits 63 s.

pitfalls: Assuming the VNI provides security: it is just a number in a cleartext header; isolation is enforced by whoever writes it (the host vswitch) and the underlay must be trusted or encrypted.
Leaving guests at MTU 1500 over a 1500-byte underlay with VXLAN: large packets are dropped, small ones (SSH, ping) work — classic "TCP handshake works, transfers hang".
Blocking ICMP "fragmentation needed / packet too big" breaks PMTUD for tunnels.

Underlay ECMP only sees outer headers; without source-port entropy all tunnel traffic between two VTEPs lands on one path.

wireless-mobile-edge.fetchNote: Gathered via web search snippets of specs, papers and vendor docs on 2026-11-14; textbook facts (Shannon, free-space loss, MIMO degrees of freedom, light in fibre) from long-stable references.

claims.text: Shannon capacity of a noisy channel: C = B·log2(1+SNR). 20 MHz at 30 dB SNR (1000×) ≈ 20·log2(1001) ≈ 199 Mb/s. Doubling bandwidth doubles C; doubling power adds only ~1 bit/s/Hz at high SNR.
Free-space received power falls with the square of distance (≈6 dB per doubling); indoors and through walls it falls faster, and multipath causes fading that varies over centimetres and milliseconds.

MIMO with Nt transmit and Nr receive antennas in rich scattering gives up to min(Nt,Nr) parallel spatial streams at high SNR, multiplying capacity; in poor scattering or low SNR the gain is diversity/beamforming instead.

Wi-Fi shares the channel with CSMA/CA: listen before talk, random backoff, link-layer ACK and retransmission. A hidden station (heard by the AP but not by another sender) causes collisions carrier sense can't prevent; RTS/CTS reserves the medium at the cost of overhead.

Link adaptation picks a modulation-and-coding scheme per frame from measured success; Linux mac80211 uses Minstrel-HT, which groups MCS rates by stream count, samples alternatives, and drops to fewer streams when multi-stream rates fail.

802.11 performance anomaly (Heusse et al. 2003): CSMA/CA gives each station an equal long-term chance to send a frame, so a slow-rate station holds the air longer per frame and drags every station's throughput down to near its own.

Høiland-Jørgensen et al. (ATC 2017) added per-station FQ-CoDel queueing and an AP-side airtime-fairness scheduler to Linux Wi-Fi (no client changes), reporting an order-of-magnitude latency reduction under load and near-perfect airtime fairness; it was merged into mainline Linux.

Wi-Fi generations: Wi-Fi 4 = 802.11n (40 MHz, 64-QAM, up to 4 streams); Wi-Fi 5 = 802.11ac (5 GHz, 160 MHz, 256-QAM, downlink MU-MIMO); Wi-Fi 6/6E = 802.11ax (OFDMA, uplink+downlink MU-MIMO, 1024-QAM, target wake time, BSS colouring; 6E adds 6 GHz); Wi-Fi 7 = 802.11be (320 MHz, 4096-QAM, multi-link operation, preamble puncturing).
IEEE Std 802.11be-2024 (Wi-Fi 7) was approved in 2024 and published 22 July 2025.

Wi-Fi 8 is IEEE 802.11bn 'Ultra High Reliability': it targets reliability (e.g. throughput at a given SINR, tail latency, loss) rather than peak rate, with multi-AP coordination as a central feature; approval is expected around 2028.

5G core (TS 23.501) is service-based: AMF handles access and mobility, SMF manages sessions, UPF forwards user traffic; the gNB is the radio node. User traffic rides a PDU session tunnelled with GTP-U over UDP from gNB (N3) to a UPF that anchors the session (PDU Session Anchor).

Network slices are identified by S-NSSAI: an 8-bit Slice/Service Type (SST) plus an optional 24-bit Slice Differentiator (SD). Standardised SSTs include 1 eMBB, 2 URLLC, 3 MIoT; a network need not support all standardised SSTs.

In an Xn handover the target gNB asks the SMF to switch the N3 path; the UPF sends an 'end marker' as the last packet on the old path so the target can drain forwarded packets before using new-path packets, preserving order.
3GPP froze Release 19 in December 2025; Release 20 combines 5G-Advanced work with 6G studies (technical reports only); the first normative 6G specifications are expected in Release 21.

Mobile IPv6 (RFC 6275, obsoletes RFC 3775): a mobile node keeps a home address; a home agent tunnels traffic to its current care-of address after a binding update; route optimization lets correspondents send directly. Without it, traffic detours via the home agent (triangle routing in MIPv4, RFC 5944).

Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213) moves mobility signalling into the network (mobile access gateway ↔ local mobility anchor) so hosts need no mobility code — the same network-anchored pattern cellular cores use.

Wi-Fi fast roaming: 802.11k gives clients neighbour reports, 802.11v lets the AP suggest a transition (the client decides), 802.11r (Fast BSS Transition) pre-derives keys so reassociation skips a full 802.1X exchange; all need AP support. Vendors cite <50 ms FT vs 0.5–1 s+ for full 802.1X re-auth.
Light in fibre travels at ~2×10^8 m/s, ~5 µs per km; 1000 km of fibre adds ~10 ms of round-trip time before any queueing or processing.

Edge computing in 5G uses local breakout: an uplink classifier (UL CL) UPF or a local PDU session anchor diverts selected flows to a nearby data network (often an ETSI MEC host); 3GPP says edge can cut latency by a factor of 2 to 10 depending on assumptions.

LoRaWAN EU868: 1% duty cycle per sub-band (36 s per hour); after a transmission of time-on-air Ta the device must stay silent Ta·(1/d − 1) = 99·Ta; DR0–DR5 = SF12..SF7 at 125 kHz; each SF step roughly doubles symbol time; max payload at SF10–12 ≈ 51 bytes.

NB-IoT and LTE-M (3GPP Release 13, 2016) target ~164 dB maximum coupling loss; PSM and eDRX let devices sleep for long periods. '10-year battery' claims hold for small, infrequent reports in good coverage; models at 164 dB give a few years for 50 bytes every 2 hours.

Constrained-device stack: IEEE 802.15.4 frames are at most 127 bytes; 6LoWPAN (RFC 4944, compression RFC 6282) compresses and fragments IPv6 to fit; CoAP (RFC 7252) is a REST protocol over UDP with a 4-byte fixed header and confirmable/non-confirmable messages; SCHC (RFC 8724) compresses and fragments for LPWANs to meet IPv6's 1280-byte MTU.
Orbit physics: LEO at ~550 km gives a bent-pipe up+down path of ~1100 km (~3.7 ms one way at c); GEO at 35,786 km gives ~240 ms one way and ~480 ms round trip before any ground segment.
Starlink reported median peak-hour latency of ~25.7 ms in the US (June 2025); laser inter-satellite links route around missing ground paths but can add latency.

Mohan et al. (WWW 2024) found globally synchronised 15-second reconfiguration intervals in Starlink that cause periodic latency and throughput degradation, contradicting the assumption that the spikes are just satellite handovers.
3GPP Release 17 introduced Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) for NR and for NB-IoT/LTE-M, handling long, changing delays and Doppler from moving satellites.
QUIC connection migration and MPTCP move mobility into the endpoints (Sheet 04), complementing network-anchored mobility.
RFC 8325 maps DSCP to 802.11 User Priority / WMM access categories (Sheet 05).

The gNB can be split into a central unit (CU) and distributed units (DU) (TS 38.401); O-RAN pushes open interfaces between them. Early 5G was often non-standalone (NR radio with an LTE/EPC core); slicing and local anchors need the 5G standalone core.
NB-IoT/LTE-M's ~164 dB MCL is roughly 20 dB beyond ordinary LTE's ~144 dB coverage target.
Motion-to-photon budgets of ~20 ms are commonly quoted for AR/VR; used only as an illustrative target.
Light in vacuum is ~1.5× faster than in glass fibre, so long laser inter-satellite paths can beat terrestrial fibre over large distances.

pitfalls: Treating wireless loss as congestion: loss-based CC backs off on fading losses; link-layer retries hide loss but add variable delay.
Packet fairness on a shared radio is not airtime fairness: one slow client slows everyone.
Peak PHY rates (e.g. Wi-Fi 7 tens of Gb/s) are not throughput: half-duplex air, MAC overhead and sharing take most of it.
Putting compute at the edge does not help if the radio hop or the session anchor dominates latency; the UPF anchor must also be local.
802.11r on with old clients can lock them out; 802.11v is advisory only.
LPWAN duty-cycle limits make downlink and acknowledgements scarce; design for uplink-mostly, unacknowledged telemetry.
Starlink latency spikes every 15 s are scheduler reconfigurations, not just handovers.
